newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's protests undimmed, shootings hit Kosovo.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's protests undimmed, shootings hit Kosovo.

text.p: Serbia's marathon mass protests against President Slobodan Milosevic showed no sign of losing momentum as violence in the communal powder keg of Kosovo province threw up a new challenge to his isolated government.

Tens of thousands of opposition supporters and students mounted separate protests in Belgrade on Saturday, both in carnival mood and both demanding for a 77th day that Milosevic must recognise opposition wins in November's local polls.

At the same time, the killing of three ethnic Albanians by Serbian police in Kosovo was a sharp reminder of the sectarian tensions that threaten to undo international peacemaking efforts across the Balkans.

The official Yugoslav news agency Tanjug, quoting the Serbian Interior Ministry, said three Serbian policemen were wounded when three men in a car shot at them on Friday. The police returned fire, killing all three men.
Tanjug said one of the dead was a commander of the clandestine Liberation Army of Kosovo and state television said weapons were found in the car of the three "outlaws".
The television also showed arms, explosives and maps of state installations which it said were seized in police raids in the mainly ethnic Albanian province over the past few days.

But Kosovo's main political party, the Democratic League of Kosovo, issued a statement saying the killings were part of a brutal Serbian crackdown involving dozens of arrests of humanitarian workers and political activists over the past week.
The League appealed to the international community to persuade the Serbian authorities to halt what it called its campaign of terror.

Ever since Milosevic abruptly cancelled Kosovo's autonomy in 1989 on grounds that the ethnic Albanians were preparing to secede, Western analysts have warned that a local flare-up in violence could ignite communal hatred across the region.
Little is known about the Liberation Army of Kosovo but it has claimed attacks over the past year in which both Serbians and ethnic Albanians have been killed.

In Belgrade, the ruling socialists appeared increasingly divided and uncertain, with more than 1,000 schools shut by striking teachers, universities in turmoil, laywers rallying with the students and no sign of an end to the mass protests.
The demonstrators have used various ways to maintain the carnival atmosphere of their street rallies, from fancy-dress parades to protests at which people turned up with their dogs.

"Tomorrow (Sunday) night please bring a stick with you," opposition poliotician Vuk Draskovic told cheering supporters, "and on top of it a placard on which you will write your wishes, and we shall read them out."
